newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: S. Leone coupmakers meet upcountry resistance.
newsitem.headline: S. Leone coupmakers meet upcountry resistance.

text.p: Soldiers loyal to Sierra Leone's coupmakers clashed upcountry with the militia of Kamajor traditional hunters as opposition to the new rulers flared in the east, military sources and witnesses said.

The new military governor of the West African nation's second city of Bo arrived on Friday to take up his post and was greeted by hundreds of people demanding the restoration of toppled civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

"We want democracy," "We do not want military rule" and "We want Tejan Kabbah back," they shouted as Major Augustine Kamara drove in a heavily-armed convoy through the streets of the southern capital of more than 700,000 people.
Military sources said several people were wounded in fighting in Ngieyema about 20 km (12 miles) from the eastern regional capital of Kenema. No official casualty figures were available.

Fourteen people -- nine civilians, three Kamajors and two soldiers -- were killed in heavy fighting between Kamajors and soldiers in the town of Joru, a few km (miles) from Ngieyema, on Thursday, witnesses said. Survivors fled to Kenema.
Military sources said more government troops were sent from Kenema to Ngieyema on Friday.
Traditional hunters are a colourful feature of life in many West African countries and they often serve as a people's militia or vigilantes to crack down on problems such as crime.

Kabbah used the Kamajor militia to fight with the army against Revolutionary United Front rebels who took up arms in 1991 and at one stage threatened to defeat the military government that preceded him.

But the Kamajors turned on the army, resulting in a string of bloody clashes, before soldiers seized power from Kabbah on May 25. The rebels have since rallied to the coup and flooded into the capital Freetown.
Leaders of the coup leaders accuse Kabbah, who is now in Guinea, of blocking peace with the rebels, humiliating the army, and promoting ethnic hatred by his use of the Kamajors.
They say they are not against democratic elections but they will not have Kabbah back. Kamajor leaders have denounced the coup and say Kabbah should be reinstated.
State radio said coup leader Johnny Paul Koroma met Kamajor leaders and traditional chiefs in Freetown on Friday and urged them to join a government of national unity.

Regional giant Nigeria, acting in the name of Sierra Leone's West African neighbours, has reinforced soldiers already in the country under a defence pact and says Kabbah should be restored to power. Nigerian gunboats stand offshore.
Kabbah took office in 1996 after multi-party elections to end four years of army rule. He signed a peace deal with rebel leader Foday Sankoh but efforts to implement it stalled.
Diplomatic sources say differences among Sierra Leone's neighbours about the way forward have put a question mark over the timing of any military action to reinstate Kabbah.
